lesson.title: Series RL and RC: impedance you can measure

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the 12 V and 16 V arrows, a quarter cycle apart, at right angles, closing a triangle whose long side matches the 20 V supply meter, when you lay them tip to tail.
interactive.title: Three meters, one triangle
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in twelve small screens on one picture, three meters and one triangle. At the top, a 6 Ω resistor and an ideal coil of about 25.5 mH sit in series on an AC supply of 20 V at 50 Hz, example values picked so the coil's reactance is 8 Ω and the numbers come out whole. An ammeter in the loop reads the current, 2 A, and three voltmeters read across the resistor, across the coil and across the supply; like ordinary AC meters on a sine wave, they read rms. Under the circuit, each part's voltage is drawn as an arrow whose length is its meter reading. One current flows through every part of a series loop, so the current is the reference and its arrow lies flat. The resistor's arrow, V_R, lies flat with it, because a resistor's voltage is in step with its current (lesson 3). The coil's arrow, V_L, starts at V_R's tip and points straight up, because an ideal coil's voltage peaks a quarter cycle before its current (lesson 4). The arrow from V_R's tail to V_L's tip closes a right-angled triangle; by Pythagoras its length is √(V_R² + V_L²), and it lands on the supply meter's reading. The angle between it and the flat side is the phase angle φ, by which the supply's voltage leads the current, with tan φ = V_L ÷ V_R. Beside the triangle, a bar shows V_R + V_L added as plain numbers, struck through, next to the supply's own bar. Readouts give the three meter readings. Screen 1 opens on the meters: 12 V across the resistor, 16 V across the coil and 20 V across the supply, with the 28 V plain-sum bar struck through. Screen 2 asks why 12 V and 16 V make 20 V, not 28 V: the two voltages peak a quarter cycle apart, so they are never both at full size together; the coil wastes 8 V as heat (an ideal coil takes no watts, lesson 4); or a smaller current flows in the coil (one series loop carries one current). A right Check plays both voltage waves on one time axis with their instant-by-instant sum, the supply's wave: the parts peak at 17.0 V and 22.6 V, but at different instants, and the sum peaks at 28.3 V, which is 20 V rms. Screen 3 turns each wave into its arrow, as in Trigonometry lesson 7, and lays them tip to tail: V_R flat, V_L straight up, and the closing side, √(12² + 16²) = 20 V, swings onto the supply meter's reading at φ = 53.13°. Screen 4 gives readings of 10 V across a resistor and 24 V across a coil in series and asks for the supply meter: 26 V; 34 V (the plain sum); or 14 V (the difference). A right Check redraws the triangle with those sides. Screen 5 turns every side from volts into ohms by dividing it by the current, 2 A: 12 V becomes R = 6 Ω, 16 V becomes X_L = 8 Ω and 20 V becomes Z = 10 Ω, the impedance. The triangle shrinks but keeps its shape and its 53.13° angle, because every side is divided by the same number. A row reads Z = √(R² + X_L²) = √(6² + 8²) = 10 Ω and I = V ÷ Z = 20 ÷ 10 = 2 A. Screen 6 starts from meters: a resistor and a coil in series on 230 V, 50 Hz mains, with the ammeter reading 5 A and the resistor's meter 200 V; what are R and X_L? 40 Ω and 22.7 Ω, from R = 200 V ÷ 5 A, Z = 230 V ÷ 5 A = 46 Ω and X_L = √(46² − 40²), and the coil's hidden meter then shows 113.6 V; 40 Ω and 6 Ω (200 V taken from 230 V as plain numbers, the 30 V divided by 5 A); or 40 Ω and 46 Ω (the whole impedance taken as the coil's reactance). Screen 7 frees a frequency slider, 0 to 100 Hz in steps of 5, opening at 50, and a resistance slider, 2 to 12 Ω in steps of 1, opening at 6 Ω, with the supply held at 20 V. Moving the resistance changes only the flat side, so Dan can see that only the reactance side depends on the frequency. The flat R side stays 6 Ω while the X_L side follows X_L = 2πfL: at 100 Hz it doubles to 16 Ω, Z reads 17.1 Ω, the current falls to 1.17 A and φ rises to 69.4°; at 25 Hz X_L is 4 Ω, Z is 7.21 Ω, the current 2.77 A and φ 33.7°; at 0 Hz, steady DC, X_L is 0 Ω, the triangle lies flat on R and the current is 20 V ÷ 6 Ω = 3.33 A. The demonstration then plays back to 50 Hz, and a dashed outline draws the resistor and the coil as one real coil whose wire has the 6 Ω. An ohmmeter's steady current makes no back-emf, so it reads only the 6 Ω; the AC meters give Z = 20 V ÷ 2 A = 10 Ω; and the triangle gives X_L = √(10² − 6²) = 8 Ω and L = 8 ÷ (2π × 50) = 25.5 mH. Screen 8: an unknown coil reads 8 Ω on an ohmmeter and draws 2 A from a 34 V, 50 Hz test supply; what is its inductance? 47.7 mH, from Z = 17 Ω and X_L = 15 Ω; 54.1 mH (all 17 Ω taken as X_L); or 28.6 mH (8 Ω taken from 17 Ω as plain numbers, leaving 9 Ω). Screen 9, back on the screen 1 bench, swaps the coil for a capacitor of about 398 µF, whose reactance at 50 Hz is also 8 Ω. The meters still read 12 V, 16 V and 20 V, but the capacitor's arrow, V_C, points straight down, because its voltage peaks a quarter cycle after its current (lesson 5). The triangle flips below the line and φ reads −53.13°: the supply's voltage lags the current. Here the triangle is drawn in volts, with the supply's side held at 20 V, so V_C shrinks and grows with X_C. On the frequency slider, now from 5 to 100 Hz, the X_C side shrinks as the frequency rises, to 4 Ω at 100 Hz, where φ reads −33.7°, and grows as it falls, to 80 Ω at 5 Hz, where the triangle stands almost on end. Screens 10 to 12 are mixed. Screen 10 sets out four ohm figures from the screen 1 bench, the ohmmeter's 6 Ω across the resistor, 16 V ÷ 2 A = 8 Ω across the coil, 16 V ÷ 2 A = 8 Ω across the capacitor and 20 V ÷ 2 A = 10 Ω across the supply, and asks which naming is right, each answer naming all three figures: resistance 6 Ω, reactances 8 Ω, impedance 10 Ω; resistance 6 Ω, reactances 10 Ω, impedance 8 Ω (the biggest figure given to the parts); or impedance 6 Ω, reactances 8 Ω, resistance 10 Ω (the ohmmeter taken as the opposition to AC). Screen 11: a 30 Ω resistor and a capacitor in series on a 50 V test supply; the resistor's meter reads 30 V; what does the capacitor's meter read? 40 V, from √(50² − 30²); 20 V (30 V taken from 50 V as plain numbers); or −40 V (the arrow below the line read as a negative reading). Screen 12: the screen 1 resistor and coil on a 20 V, 60 Hz supply, the frequency most common on board ship. The current is 1.77 A, lagging by 58.0°, from X_L = 9.6 Ω and Z = 11.3 Ω; or 1.67 A, lagging by 53.1° (the whole 10 Ω scaled up with the frequency, resistance and all); or 2 A, lagging by 53.1° (the frequency ignored). Each puzzle offers three answers; a wrong pick gets a one-line hint naming its slip, Why? explains in words, and a right Check draws the answer on the picture. The closing line says the meters disagree with plain arithmetic because the part voltages peak a quarter cycle apart, and that lesson 7 puts a coil and a capacitor in one loop, where their arrows point opposite ways.
interactive.ignores: The resistor is a pure resistance and the coil and the capacitor are ideal, so the arrows sit at exactly right angles; a real coil's own wire resistance tips its arrow a little off the vertical, which is why screen 7 treats a real coil as a resistance and an ideal coil in one body. The meters are ideal: they draw nothing and read the true rms of a pure sine. The arrows are drawn to the rms readings where Trigonometry drew peaks; both give the same triangle, because every side is scaled by the same √2. Nothing physical points up or down: the directions stand for timing, and only the angles between arrows mean anything. A coil with an iron core also loses some energy in the iron on AC, and its inductance changes with its current; treating that loss as extra resistance an ohmmeter cannot see is our own reasoning from the triangle's rule, not from a source. The switch-on surge is left out. The parts, the supplies and the readings are example values.

explain.text:
Put a resistor and a coil in series on AC and meter each one, and the two readings add up to more than the supply meter shows: 12 V across the resistor, 16 V across the coil, yet 20 V across the supply. Nothing is lost. The two voltages peak a quarter cycle apart, so they add as arrows at right angles, and the supply's voltage is the long side of the right-angled triangle they make. Divide every side by the current and the same triangle gives the circuit's resistance, its reactance and its whole opposition to AC, which is how an ohmmeter, a voltmeter and an ammeter find an unknown coil's inductance.

In a series loop one current flows through every part, so the current is what the parts share. The resistor's voltage is in step with that current (lesson 3). The ideal coil's voltage peaks a quarter cycle earlier, because its back-emf follows how fast the current is changing (lesson 4), and a quarter cycle is a quarter turn of Trigonometry's arm, a right angle. At every instant the supply's voltage is the resistor's plus the coil's at that instant, just as on DC. But when the resistor's voltage is at its peak the coil's is passing through zero, and the other way round, so the two are never both at full size together, and their sum peaks lower than their two peaks added. Trigonometry lesson 7 showed how to add two such waves: their sum is itself a sine wave of the same frequency, and drawing each as an arrow and laying them tip to tail gives it, because the closing arrow is the sum. With the current's arrow lying flat, the resistor's arrow lies flat too and the coil's points straight up, so the closing arrow is the long side of a right-angled triangle, and Pythagoras gives its length. A meter reads rms, and all three are sine waves, so every reading is its wave's peak ÷ √2; shrinking every side by the same √2 keeps the triangle's shape, so the readings make the same triangle: √(12² + 16²) = 20 V. A textbook adds a 6 V source to an 8 V source a quarter cycle apart the same way, and gets 10 V at a phase angle of 53.13°.[^3] The 12 V and 16 V here are those doubled, so the closing arrow sits at the same 53.13° above the flat side: the supply's voltage leads the current by that angle, φ.

Each side is the current times something. The resistor's voltage is I × R, the coil's is I × X_L, and the supply's is I × the circuit's whole opposition to AC, its [[impedance]], Z, in ohms. Divide every side by the same 2 A and the triangle shrinks without changing shape: 6 Ω of resistance lying flat, 8 Ω of inductive reactance standing up, and Z = √(R² + X_L²) = 10 Ω along the long side,[^4] still at 53.13°. This is the [[impedance triangle]] of Complex numbers lesson 7's Z = R + jX, here 6 + j8 = 10∠53.13°, now read off meters. It turns an unknown coil into numbers. A real coil's wire resistance and inductance sit in one body, so no meter can be put across one without the other. But an ohmmeter's steady current makes no back-emf, so it reads the wire's resistance alone (lesson 4); a voltmeter and an ammeter on AC give Z = V ÷ I; Pythagoras gives X_L = √(Z² − R²); and X_L = 2πfL[^5] gives L. In this model only the reactance side depends on the frequency, so a higher frequency stands the coil's triangle taller and a lower one lays it flatter, until on steady DC only R is left.

Swap the coil for a capacitor of the same reactance and the meters read exactly the same, but its voltage peaks a quarter cycle after the current (lesson 5), so its arrow points straight down and the triangle flips below the line: φ is −53.13°, and the supply's voltage lags the current. Its side runs the other way with frequency too, shrinking as the frequency rises and growing as it falls (lesson 5), so towards steady DC the capacitor's triangle stands almost on end. This is a simplified model, with a pure resistor and an ideal coil or capacitor on a pure sine; an iron-cored coil also loses some energy in its iron on AC, which an ohmmeter cannot see. Reasoning from the triangle's own rule, not from a source: if that loss acts as extra resistance, the true R is larger, so the true X is smaller and the inductance found this way comes out a little high. **In series, a resistor's voltage and a coil's or a capacitor's add as arrows at right angles, so the supply meter reads √(V_R² + V_X²), and dividing every side by the current turns the same triangle into R, X and the impedance Z = √(R² + X²).[^4]**

analogy.text: Run a cable 12 m along one wall of a plant room and then 16 m along the next wall, round the corner. The tape along the cable reads 28 m, yet the straight line from start to finish, across the room, is 20 m, because the two runs are at right angles. The meters across the resistor and the coil are the tape on each run; the supply meter measures the straight line.
analogy.breaks: The cable's runs are at right angles in space, and you could walk them. The voltage arrows are at right angles in time: the angle stands for the quarter cycle between their peaks, and nothing physical points up. And the meter readings change with the frequency, while a cable's runs stay the same length.

practice.text:
- Isolate and prove dead before the ohmmeter test. On a large coil, keep clear of the terminals as the leads come off: cutting even the meter's small current quickly can give a sharp kick of back-emf (lesson 4).
- Ohmmeter across the coil: its wire's resistance, R.
- On AC, read the voltage across the coil and the current through it, both rms: Z = V ÷ I.
- The reactance: X_L = √(Z² − R²). Square both, take one from the other, then take the square root.[^4]
- The inductance: L = X_L ÷ (2πf), with f in hertz, gives henries.[^5]
- The angle: tan φ = X ÷ R, with X the coil's or the capacitor's reactance. For a coil the current lags by φ; for a capacitor it leads.

**Rule of thumb:** With a resistor and one coil or one capacitor in series, the supply meter reads less than the two part readings added and more than either one. Square, add, square root.

**Worked example:** An example coil reads 15 Ω on an ohmmeter and draws 10 A from 230 V, 50 Hz mains.[^1] Z = 230 ÷ 10 = 23 Ω. X_L = √(23² − 15²) = √304 ≈ 17.44 Ω. L = 17.44 ÷ (2 × π × 50) ≈ 0.0555 H, or 55.5 mH. The current lags the voltage by the angle whose tangent is 17.44 ÷ 15, which is 49.3°. On a 230 V, 60 Hz supply (60 Hz is the frequency most common on board ship[^2]), X_L rises to 20.9 Ω while R stays 15 Ω, so Z = √(15² + 20.9²) ≈ 25.7 Ω and the current falls to 8.93 A.

Lesson 7 puts a coil and a capacitor in one loop, where their arrows point opposite ways, and lesson 8 turns the angle φ into the power factor.

**Common mistakes**
- Adding the part voltages, or the ohms, as plain numbers. 12 V and 16 V at right angles make 20 V, and 6 Ω and 8 Ω make 10 Ω.
- Taking Z = V ÷ I as the coil's reactance. Take the resistance out first, by Pythagoras.
- Taking R from Z as plain numbers. In the worked example, 23 Ω less 15 Ω leaves 17.44 Ω of reactance by Pythagoras, not 8 Ω.
- Reading a capacitor's arrow below the line as a negative meter reading. The meter shows the size; the arrow's direction shows the timing.
- Scaling the whole impedance with the frequency. Only the reactance changes; the resistance stays put.
- Taking an ohmmeter's reading as a coil's opposition to AC. It misses the reactance.

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the 12 V and 16 V arrows, a quarter cycle apart, at right angles, closing a triangle whose long side matches the 20 V supply meter, when you lay them tip to tail.

checks.label: A 6 volt source at 0° added to an 8 volt source at 90° results in 10 volts at a phase angle of 53.13°: laid tip to tail at right angles, 6 V and 8 V close on 10 V at 53.13°, and the drawn 12 V and 16 V arrows close on the 20 V supply at the same angle

Because the phasors for reactances are 90° out of phase with the current, the series impedance of a resistor R and a reactance X is given by Pythagoras' law: on every screen, and at every setting of both frequency sliders and the resistance slider, the drawn closing side is √(flat² + upright²) and the upright stands square on the flat side's tip

Inductive reactance can be calculated using this formula: X_L = 2πfL. On the frequency screen the drawn X_L side, its rows and the meters agree with it at every setting from 0 to 100 Hz, and the demonstration ends back at 50 Hz, where a real coil's rows find 25.5 mH
60 Hz is the most common frequency adopted for use on board ship: answered, the ship screen runs the first bench at 60 Hz, where X_L is 9.6 Ω, Z is 11.3 Ω and 1.77 A flows, lagging 58.0°
UK mains electricity operates at a nominal voltage of 230V: on 230 V with 5 A flowing and 200 V across the resistor, R is 40 Ω, Z is 46 Ω and X_L is 22.7 Ω, and the coil's meter reads 113.6 V

Screen 2's supply wave is the resistor's plus the coil's at every drawn instant: the parts peak at 17.0 V and 22.6 V a quarter cycle apart (the coil's is at zero when the resistor's peaks), and the sum peaks at 28.3 V, which is 20 V rms

The bench reads 12 V, 16 V and 20 V at 50 Hz and draws 2 A; at 100 Hz Z is 17.1 Ω and 1.17 A flows at 69.4°; at 25 Hz 7.21 Ω, 2.77 A and 33.7°; at 0 Hz 3.33 A; with the 398 µF capacitor, 100 Hz gives X_C = 4 Ω at −33.7° and 5 Hz gives 80 Ω
Dividing every side by the 2 A current turns 12 V, 16 V and 20 V into R = 6 Ω, X_L = 8 Ω and Z = 10 Ω: the drawn triangle halves but keeps its 53.13° angle

The plain-sum bar is V_R + V_X long and the supply bar the supply's reading, on the arrows' scale; the swung closing side lands on the supply bar's end; with the capacitor both bars follow the frequency
With the capacitor its arrow points down: at 50 Hz the meters still read 12.0 V, 16.0 V and 20.0 V and φ is −53.13°; at 5 Hz the triangle stands almost on end at −85.7°
